Project Praxis, with ZZTong's Prefabs, is an overhaul for 7 Days to Die. It changes where your character comes from: you no longer spend points on a build, you arrive at one by using the skills you want. Praxis means knowledge put into practice - what you can do, rather than what you know on paper.

THIS IS A PROOF OF CONCEPT. It is playable, and it is being played, but it is not finished and it is not balanced. Progression rates especially are still being tuned - they have already moved a long way once - and nothing here promises that a world you start today will survive the next update. Treat a save in this pack as one you are willing to lose.

That cuts both ways, and it is the useful part. If a skill climbs absurdly fast, or sits still for a whole day while you work at it, that is worth saying out loud rather than quietly playing around. Finding those is what this build is for.

None of that makes the game easier in the ordinary sense. Zombies hit as hard as they always did, the blood moon still comes, and the world is still trying to kill you. What changes is how you get good at surviving it.

Around that sits a layer of quality of life meant to remove chores rather than difficulty, and a set of comfort changes for players who want the survival without some of the horror dressing.

The map is broader too. ZZTong's Prefabs widens the pool world generation draws from, so the places you clear are far less predictable than on a stock map.

The other two tabs cover all of this in turn. If you only read one thing first, read Progression - it is the part that will feel unfamiliar, and the part worth understanding before you start rather than an hour in.

SKILLS COME FROM USE. Swing a club and you get better with clubs. Mine ore and you get better at mining. Every perk levels itself from the actions it governs, and the attribute above it rises from anything in its tree - so committing to a few perks pulls their parent up with them.

YOU CANNOT BUY ANY OF IT. Perks and attributes are no longer for sale, and levelling up awards no skill points to spend. The skill window becomes somewhere you look at what you have earned rather than somewhere you shop.

SKILLS FADE IF YOU ABANDON THEM. Every skill carries a hidden inactivity timer. Stop using something long enough and it slips back down. This is the part to plan around: a wide, shallow character is harder to hold together than a narrow, deep one, because everything you are not currently doing is quietly cooling off.

The practical shape of this is that your first few days decide a lot. Pick the weapon you actually enjoy and use it, rather than saving it for later.

Levelling still matters even without points to spend - level requirements, attribute caps and perk prerequisites are all unchanged, so your level still governs what you are allowed to reach. The Challenges tab covers where the extra experience comes from.

Full detail on any of this is in the game: press ESC and choose Mod Help.

FEWER CHORES. Crafting reads from containers near you, so materials no longer have to be hauled into your own inventory first. Block upgrades and repairs read from them too - though not while enemies are close, because shoring up a base is something you do between fights rather than during one.

The Drop Box sorts for you. Anything put inside is moved out into nearby containers that already hold that item, so unloading after a run is one drop rather than a sorting session. It comes in wood, iron and steel.

Books are shared across a party, so a group does not need to find duplicates of the same volume.

EASIER TO LOOK AT. Camera and weapon sway are switched off, so the view sits still and the weapon points where you are aiming - the usual reason people give up on first person survival games. Flickering and pulsing lights in points of interest hold steady. Whatever you are aiming at shows a health bar.

LESS TO FLINCH AT. Scenes implying that a person killed another person, or took their own life, are removed - the bodies hung from posts, and the noose. Ordinary death is left alone: corpses, blood and bones are all still there, because a body that fell to the outbreak says nothing about anyone having done it to them. Language is softened, and one trader has been persuaded to be civil.

Chuck and the Rancher have lost their ranged attacks and have to reach you to hurt you.

A WIDER WORLD. Locked containers can be picked with a minigame instead of simply refusing you.

More noticeably, the map is built from a much larger pool of locations. That comes from ZZTong Prefabs, a separate modlet by ZZTong bundled into this pack, which adds over two hundred new points of interest, around a hundred and twenty roadside decorations and a set of new city tiles. World generation mixes them in with the stock ones on its own - nothing needs configuring, generate a world and they are in it.

Two things worth knowing about them. The decorations are scenery rather than quest locations, and they do not take the place of anything, so having them costs you no POIs. And some of the hunters' traps scattered among them are genuinely lethal, so treat an unfamiliar contraption in the woods with more respect than it appears to deserve.

If you are playing on a server, this pack needs to be installed on the server and on every client. Server side alone mostly works, but location names and some trigger wiring will not reach you.

Around eighty extra challenges sit alongside the ones the game ships with, in three new categories.

ABILITY, the largest at about fifty. These follow the five attributes, and most ask for ten kills with one particular weapon - each rifle, each club, each bow, and so on down every tree. A bonus group alongside them asks for stealth instead: sneak kills with melee and with ranged, then streaks where the kills have to come one after another without you being spotted.

SCORE, about twenty, for the things that have nothing to do with what you are holding. Taking heads with blade, gun and bow. Crafting with particular ingredients. Starting fires, keeping a large one going, and putting fires out. Harvesting with an axe. Gathering junk, wearing armour, and clearing every sleeper out of a point of interest.

NPC, eight of them, for hiring companions. THESE CANNOT BE COMPLETED IN THIS PACK - they need an NPC mod to supply someone to hire, and none is installed. The category is listed and its challenges are visible, but nothing in it will ever tick over. It is left in place so the challenges are there if you add an NPC pack yourself.

Most pay a thousand experience, and they redeem themselves the moment you finish them - there is no trip back to the challenge window to claim anything.

That experience is still worth having. Levelling no longer hands you points to spend, but level requirements, attribute caps and perk prerequisites are all unchanged, so your level still decides what you are allowed to reach.

A few entries in the SCore category are development tests rather than real challenges, and show placeholder text where their description should be.
